title: Hats returned at random
objectives: Find the expected number of people who get their own hat back.

screens.title: Whose hat?
screens.prose: Four people check their hats. The hats come back in a random order, one to each person. A **match** is a person who gets their own hat.

state.caption: Each card is a hat, lettered by its owner: A is Ann's, B is Bo's, and so on.

screens.question: Tap every hat that went back to its owner.

hints.text: Compare each hat's letter with the name above it.
Bo and Dev hold their own hats.

feedback.correct: Bo has B and Dev has D: two matches.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A match is a hat whose letter starts its owner's name.

byKey.one: Bo has his own hat. Look at Dev too.
byKey.one-d: Dev has his own hat. Look at Bo too.
byKey.hA: Hat A is Ann's, but Cai has it.
byKey.hC: Hat C is Cai's, but Ann has it.

explain.text: This shuffle has two matches, Bo and Dev. Another shuffle could have none, or all four. We want the average count over every shuffle.

screens.title: Expected matches
screens.prose: Every hat is equally likely to go to any person, so Ann gets her own hat with chance $\tfrac14$. The same holds for each person: that is **symmetry**.

state.caption: Each card is a hat, lettered by its owner: A is Ann's, B is Bo's, and so on.

screens.question: How many matches do you expect with four people?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add one indicator per person, each with chance $\tfrac14$.

byKey.one: That is one person's chance. Add it over all four people.
byKey.this: That is this shuffle. The question asks for the average over all shuffles.

explain.text: Each person matches with chance $\tfrac14$, so $E[\text{matches}] = 4 \times \tfrac14 = 1$. The same argument gives $n \times \tfrac1n = 1$ for any $n$. Symmetry gives each chance, and linearity adds them.

screens.title: Count the shuffles
screens.prose: The table lists all 24 ways to hand back four hats, with the matches in each.

state.caption: "BADC" means Ann gets B, Bo gets A, Cai gets D and Dev gets C.

screens.question: Count the orderings with each number of matches.

hints.text: Nine orderings have no match and eight have one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count down the Matches columns of the table.

byKey.r3c1: Three matches would leave one hat for its own owner, so a fourth match is forced. Exactly three never happens.
byKey.r0c1: Count the rows with 0 in either Matches column: there are nine.

explain.text: The counts are 9, 8, 6, 0 and 1. Exactly three matches is impossible: the last hat must then go to its owner. As a check, $(8 \cdot 1 + 6 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 4)/24 = 1$, the expected matches again.

screens.title: No match at all
screens.prose: Now find the chance that nobody gets their own hat. Check it a second way, by inclusion and exclusion: $$24 - \tbinom41 3! + \tbinom42 2! - \tbinom43 1! + \tbinom44 0!.$$

state.caption: "BADC" means Ann gets B, Bo gets A, Cai gets D and Dev gets C.

screens.question: What is the chance of no match with four people? Give three decimal places.

hints.text: How many orderings have no match?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the orderings with no match by 24.

byKey.count: That is the count of orderings. Divide by all 24.
byKey.third: That is the chance of exactly one match, $8/24$.
byKey.more: That is the chance of at least one match.

explain.text: Both counts give 9 of 24, so the chance is $\tfrac38 = 0.375$. Inclusion and exclusion counts orderings that fix at least one named person, then corrects the overlaps. It works for any $n$, where listing does not.

screens.title: A thousand hats
screens.prose: With more people there are more chances for someone to match. A candidate concludes that with 1,000 people, somebody surely gets their own hat.
screens.question: What is the chance that nobody gets their own hat with 1,000 people?

options.why: More people means more chances, but each chance shrinks to $\tfrac1n$. The expected number of matches stays 1.
Each person rarely matches, but there are 1,000 of them. One match is expected on average.
That is one person's chance of a match.

hints.text: What is the expected number of matches for any $n$?
It is always 1. The chart swings less as $n$ grows.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The expected number of matches is 1 for every $n$.

byKey.b: You let the number of chances grow without letting each one shrink. The expected matches is 1 for every $n$, so no match stays likely.

explain.text: For 5 to 8 people the chance is 0.367, 0.368, 0.368 and 0.368. The series $1 - 1 + \tfrac1{2!} - \tfrac1{3!} + \dots$ converges to $1/e \approx 0.3679$. More people bring more chances, each smaller, and the two effects balance.

screens.title: Symmetry and indicators
screens.prose:
With $n$ people, symmetry gives each person chance $\tfrac1n$, and linearity adds: 

$$E[\text{matches}] = n \cdot \tfrac1n = 1$$

$$P(\text{no match}) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^k}{k!} \to \frac1e$$
screens.question: Why does each person get their own hat with chance exactly $\tfrac1n$?

options.text: Their hat is equally likely to go to any of the $n$ people

options.why: They are not: if $n - 1$ people match, the last must too. Symmetry alone gives $\tfrac1n$.
That is the conclusion, not the reason. It follows from each chance being $\tfrac1n$.

feedback.correct: Symmetry: no person is special, so each gets any given hat with chance $\tfrac1n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where one person's hat can go.

explain.text: A random handing back treats every person alike, so your hat lands with you one time in $n$. Adding $n$ such chances gives 1. Symmetry gave the chance; linearity did the rest.

screens.title: The spread is 1 too
screens.prose: Interviewers often follow up: what is the variance of the number of matches? Build it from pairs of indicators.
screens.question: Put the derivation in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Write $N = I_1 + \dots + I_n$, with $I_i = 1$ when person $i$ gets their own hat.
Square: $N^2 = \sum_i I_i + \sum_{i \ne j} I_iI_j$, since $I_i^2 = I_i$.

hints.text: Squaring gives single terms and pair terms.
Sum, square, pair chance, pair count, then $2 - 1 = 1$.

feedback.correct: Indicators, square, pair chance, count the pairs, subtract.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the sum before taking expectations.

byKey.d1: The matches are dependent. Once person $i$ has their hat, $n - 1$ hats remain for $n - 1$ people.
byKey.left-out: Every true line is needed: the pair chance and the pair count both feed $E[N^2]$.
byKey.s5: The variance comes last, once $E[N^2]$ is known.

explain.text: The pair chance $\tfrac1{n(n - 1)}$ times $n(n - 1)$ ordered pairs gives exactly 1. So $E[N^2] = 2$ and $\text{Var}(N) = 1$ for every $n \ge 2$. For large $n$ the count is close to a Poisson count with mean 1.

screens.title: Reconciling at random
screens.prose: A back office holds 50 trades and 50 confirmations, one for each trade. A faulty script pairs them up at random before the real check runs.
screens.question: How many trades do you expect to be paired with their own confirmation?

hints.text: This is the hat problem with 50 people.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each trade finds its own confirmation with chance $\tfrac1{50}$.

byKey.rate: That is one trade's chance. There are 50 trades.
byKey.half: You gave each trade an even chance. It has 50 confirmations to land on.

explain.text: One correct pairing is expected by chance, whatever the book's size. With chance about $1/e \approx 0.37$ none line up at all. So a handful of matches proves nothing about the script.

ideas: By symmetry each person gets their own hat with chance $\tfrac1n$.
So the expected number of matches is 1 for every $n$, and its variance is 1 too.
The chance of no match settles at $1/e \approx 0.368$; it never goes to 0.

formula.name: Matches in a random handing back

summary.trap: Thinking more people means a match becomes certain. Each chance shrinks as the number of chances grows.

quiz.prose: Eight people with numbered tickets sit down at random in eight numbered seats.
quiz.question: How many people do you expect to sit in their own seat?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One indicator per person, each with chance $\tfrac18$.

byKey.half: You gave each person an even chance of their own seat.

explain.text: Each person lands in their own seat with chance $\tfrac18$, so one person is expected. It is the hat problem with seats.

quiz.prose: Five people check their hats and get them back at random.
quiz.question: What is the chance that nobody gets their own hat? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use inclusion and exclusion on $5! = 120$ orderings.

byKey.e: That is the limit $1/e$. For five people the exact chance is $\tfrac{44}{120}$.

explain.text: $120 - 120 + 60 - 20 + 5 - 1 = 44$ orderings have no match, so $44/120 \approx 0.3667$. It is already within 0.002 of $1/e$.

quiz.prose: Shuffle two decks separately and turn their cards over together, one pair at a time.
quiz.question: How many times do you expect the two cards to be identical?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At each of the 52 turns, the two cards agree with chance $\tfrac1{52}$.

byKey.rate: That is one turn's chance. There are 52 turns.
byKey.zero: Matches are not rare: one is expected.

explain.text: At each turn the second deck's card is the first deck's card with chance $\tfrac1{52}$. Over 52 turns that is 1 expected match, the hat problem again.

quiz.prose: One person checks one hat and gets a hat back.
quiz.question: What are the expected number of matches and the chance of no match?

options.why: The limit $1/e$ needs many people. With one person the only hat is theirs.
There is only one hat, so it must be theirs.

feedback.correct: One person always gets their own hat: 1 match, and no chance of none.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With one hat there is only one way to hand it back.

explain.text: The formula gives $1 \times \tfrac11 = 1$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{1} (-1)^k/k! = 1 - 1 = 0$. This is the edge case, $n = 1$.
